title: Pydantic
summary: Type hints as a runtime schema: parsing and coercion, collected validation errors, constraints and validators, settings from the environment, and what changed in v2.

clips.title: Parse, don't just check
clips.question: What does a Pydantic model do with input like id="123", and with bad input?

scenes.say: Pydantic, question one. You define a model with an integer id, and pass it the string one two three. What happens? And what happens with input that can't be fixed? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: A model gets id="123", then garbage. What happens?

scenes.say: A model is a class whose type hints are the schema. Pydantic parses rather than just checking: the string one two three becomes the integer one two three. When input can't be converted, it raises a validation error, and it collects every failure at once, each with its field location and a message, instead of stopping at the first.

props.title: Type hints are the schema
props.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str
    is_active: bool = True

u = User(id="123", name="Ada", email="ada@example.com")
u.id                       # 123: the string was coerced to int

try:
    User(id="abc", name=None)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)               # every failure, with its location:
    # id     Input should be a valid integer
    # name   Input should be a valid string
    # email  Field required

highlights.note: All errors at once, with locations

scenes.say: That conversion is lax mode, the default. If you'd rather reject a string where an integer is expected, switch the model to strict mode: now one two three as a string is an error. Strict is useful at trust boundaries where silent conversion would hide bugs.

right.label: Strict
right.title: Exact types only
right.code:
class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
    id: int

User(id="123")      # ValidationError

verdict.text: Strict where silent conversion would hide bugs.

clips.title: Constraints and validators
clips.question: How do you express rules like price > 0, or passwords must match?

scenes.say: Question two. How do you express rules like price must be positive, normalize an email, or passwords must match? Pause and answer out loud.

Simple rules are declarative: Field takes constraints like a minimum length, or greater than zero. A mutable default like an empty list is safe, because Pydantic copies it for each instance. For custom logic on one field, use a field validator: it can transform the value, and whatever it returns replaces the input. For rules across fields, like matching passwords, use a model validator in after mode: it runs on the fully validated model, so every field is available.

clips.title: Settings, serialization, and v2
clips.question: How do you load config from the environment, serialize models, and what changed in Pydantic v2?

scenes.say: Question three. How do you load configuration from environment variables, how do you serialize a model, and what changed in Pydantic version two? Pause and answer out loud.

Base settings, from the pydantic settings package, reads each field from an environment variable, or a dot env file, and validates it like any model: the string true becomes a boolean. To go back out, model dump gives a dict, model dump json a JSON string, and model json schema the JSON Schema that FastAPI turns into its API docs.

props.title: Settings in, JSON out
props.code:
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")
    db_url: str
    api_key: str
    debug: bool = False                  # DEBUG=true in the env → True

settings = Settings()                    # reads env vars + .env, validates

u.model_dump()                           # → dict
u.model_dump_json()                      # → JSON string
User.model_json_schema()                 # → JSON Schema (FastAPI's OpenAPI)

scenes.say: Version two rewrote the core in Rust, as pydantic core, which made validation several times to tens of times faster. And the API was renamed: dict became model dump; parse obj became model validate; validator became field validator; and the inner Config class became a model config attribute.

items.label: Core
items.title: pydantic-core
items.body: Validation rewritten in Rust; much faster.

scenes.say: To recap. Type hints are the schema, and Pydantic parses, coercing when it's safe. It reports every error at once. Use Field for declarative rules, and validators for custom and cross-field ones. And load settings from the environment with base settings.
